Vantor/Handout via REUTERS China’s new joint air training facility in Laos highlights Beijing’s incremental expansion of its military access across Southeast Asia. The 2,000-meter runway could extend the operational reach of Chinese aircraft, although its current capabilities remain limited and its long-term purpose is uncertain. Unlike a conventional overseas base, the facility reflects a gradual approach to expanding China’s regional security footprint.
The bigger story may be Beijing’s deepening political and economic influence in Laos, where Chinese investment, debt exposure, and growing party-to-party ties strengthen bilateral relations. As Japan expands security cooperation across Southeast Asia and the United States maintains its regional military presence, China’s evolving access arrangements could gradually reshape the regional balance of power.
Hunter Marston, director of the Southeast Asia Program at the Lowy Institute and project lead for the Asia Power Index, joins Eric to talk about China’s military ambitions in Laos, the strategic implications of its growing regional access, and the roles of economic leverage and Japan’s expanding security partnerships.
Dr. Hunter Marston is the Director of the Southeast Asia Program at the Lowy Institute and Project Lead for the Asia Power Index. His research focuses on great power competition in Southeast Asia, Indo-Pacific security and alliances, and U.S. foreign policy, with particular attention to the evolving strategic dynamics shaping the region.
Marston is also an Adjunct Nonresident Fellow with the Center for Strategic and International Studies’ Southeast Asia Program, an Adjunct Research Fellow at La Trobe Asia, and an Associate with 9DashLine. He holds a PhD in International Relations from the Australian National University, a master’s degree in Southeast Asian Studies, and a Master of Public Administration from the University of Washington.
Previously, Marston worked with the Brookings Institution’s Center for East Asia Policy Studies and the Center for Strategic and International Studies. His analysis and commentary have appeared in Foreign Affairs , Foreign Policy , The New York Times , The Washington Post , and other leading academic and international publications.
ERIC OLANDER: Hello, and welcome to another edition of the China Global South podcast, a proud member of the Sinica podcast network. I’m Eric Olander. For many years, there’s been mounting concern, especially in the United States, that China is seeking to build military bases around the world.
Every year, the Pentagon submits a report to Congress on its assessment of the PLA, and every year they include a long list of countries that China is purportedly considering where it wants to build some military outpost. We’ve talked a lot on this show about how much of that rhetoric coming out of the Pentagon is just sheer fantasy, and how it’s a little odd that a country with more than 800 bases around the world is concerned about a rival that up until recently just had one. Well, China’s overseas count has gone up recently, and it’s now somewhere between one and three.
There’s the base in Djibouti, which by the conventional definition is a proper military base. Then there’s a joint Cambodian naval facility at the Ream Naval Base. Calling that facility, calling the PLA’s operations there a base, is probably overstating it, but they definitely have an ongoing presence there.
And then we learned a few weeks ago that the PLA Air Force built a joint military support and training facility at the Bangun airport in Laos, near the Thai border. Now, we don’t know much about the facility, but satellite images have revealed a few clues. There’s a 2,000-meter-long runway with parking spaces for roughly two dozen aircraft.
So far, we haven’t seen any of China’s advanced fighter jets like the J-10s or the JF-16s. Instead, what we see from the satellite pictures are JL-8 trainer and light attack jets that are used by both the Chinese and the Laotians. But again, none of China’s more sophisticated fighter jets and certainly none of the larger jets that are probably not compatible with that airstrip.
China, for its part, denies that it’s a formal Air Force base and instead insists that the facility is intended to train Lao Air Force pilots and foster closer security cooperation with its southern neighbor. Well, let’s find out more from someone who’s been following this story very closely. Hunter Marston is the director of the Southeast Asia Program at the Lowy Institute, and project lead for the Asia Power Index.
Shortly after the base in Laos was announced, he wrote a fascinating article for The Interpreter, What to Make of China’s New Air Facility in Laos. And he joins us today to help us all figure it out. Hunter, good afternoon to you and thanks so much for joining us.
HUNTER MARSTON: Good afternoon, Eric. Thank you very much for having me on the show.
ERIC OLANDER: Let’s start with what is this thing? Is it a base? Is it a training
HUNTER MARSTON: I think it’s too early to say for certain how this facility will be used in the longer-term. Right now, both sides have described it as a joint air training center. It’s about 2,000 meters long, which is long enough to land most of the fighter jets in China’s PLA Air Force arsenal.
But it’s short of the length required to launch longer-range bombers like the H-6. Joint statement, which announced the opening of the facility mentioned that it will be used for aviation training of Laos Air Force, which is very nascent and limited in its own capabilities and resources. But the air center seems more generally to be a just infrastructure with potential to grow in the future at this point. And the longer-term implications of it remain uncertain at this point.
ERIC OLANDER: Why do you think China chose Laos more than, say, other countries in the
region? Is it just the opportunity? Is there something strategic about it? Why Laos?
HUNTER MARSTON: Well, a couple of reasons. You mentioned in your introductory remarks,
the Ream Naval Base in Cambodia, which was upgraded in 2019 with Chinese funding. Now that naval facility expands Chinese access, but it’s also been open to other navies, including the United States and Japan.
So it doesn’t seem to be an exclusive Chinese base. Cambodia’s politics have shifted somewhat in the last decade. And the Trump and Biden administrations before it have both invested considerable attention in pulling Phnom Penh away from the Chinese orbit.
And I think the leadership in Phnom Penh also recognizes that too much reliance on China potentially exposes them to coercion and unwanted leverage from or intervention from Beijing. So Cambodia’s politics have shifted to an extent that I think, makes it less attractive to seek to take advantage of and form or put new bases in. Laos, on the other hand,
is relatively open to Chinese investment and infrastructure.
The political ties between the Lao Revolutionary Party and the Communist Party of China are significant and growing. And I think Laos is seen as the natural partner for such a new endeavor for China’s military expansion in Southeast Asia. It also positions China’s operational or gives it extended range further southwest, potentially allowing it to
Now, again, we don’t know the long-term usage of the Banquan air facility. So it could be that China is using it for training, using it to support its own multilateral or bilateral military exercises with other Southeast Asian countries. But it also allows the prepositioning
of certain assets that would allow it to reach more easily the Indian Ocean and further into South Asia.
ERIC OLANDER: What are some of the security concerns that China would be trying to address with a base like this? So you talk about prepositioning security assets and Air Force assets in Laos towards the Indian Ocean. What are they trying to repel with a base like this or with a facility like this?
HUNTER MARSTON: It’s not so much about what they seek to repel. I think it’s more about
expanding the deployment capabilities of Chinese jets, so they can get to quickly. China’s ultimate goal is probably to push out the U.S. security presence. Right now, the U.S. has rotational access in a number of countries, including Thailand and Singapore, as well as bases in the Philippines and further afield in Guam and Okinawa. So the U.S. essentially has China encircled already. China is, from a defensive standpoint, trying to incrementally expand its own reach and its ability to fly over and monitor other events in its near abroad,
Now the runways, and we could get to this perhaps in a bit, but the artificial islands it’s constructed in the South China Sea have significantly larger runways and hardware and facilities and infrastructure that allow for the basing and placement of long-range bombers, which it has already done. So the capabilities of the Banquan facility are actually significantly limited by comparison.
ERIC OLANDER: Yeah. So if we look now at Chinese force projection in the region, we’ve
got the South China Sea islands that, as you mentioned, are now heavily
militarized and can take heavy bombers. There is something in Ring.
Again, we don’t really understand the full extent of it, but as you pointed out, and as we’ve noticed, there is some ongoing presence by the PLA Navy there. And then now with Laos, what do you think the ultimate goal is? And particularly for a country like Vietnam now, they must be feeling a little bit anxious given the fact that there’s now a Chinese military presence to their north, to their west, and to their east.
Tell us a little bit about the scattershot now of the Chinese military
HUNTER MARSTON: the long-term implications or the agenda, it’s anybody’s guess. But
essentially, China has pursued what you call a scattershot approach that involves a little bit of hedging your bets. They’re not going all in on any one of these.
So partial access, and sometimes this is pursued in conjunction with regular commercial port infrastructure development. Perhaps, the example of Sri Lanka from about 10 years ago is one case that comes to mind. But other times we see something like this joint training facility, which has the potential for greater Chinese exclusive access down their line.
Right now, it’s not that. But China owns, I think, a third of all of Laos’s external debt. It’s the largest owner of Chinese debt.
It has the potential to place political leverage and economic coercion on Laos to extract certain concessions if it wants to down the road. At this point, I’m not sure that that’s the goal. But now it has little pieces of territory or access in different countries around its
ERIC OLANDER: Have you seen any evidence of China leveraging its debt relationships,
not only in Southeast Asia, but elsewhere, to maximize the security engagements? Or is that speculation?
ERIC OLANDER: Yeah, that’s what, because we haven’t seen the evidence of it. And I was
HUNTER MARSTON: No, there’s nothing exactly that I would point to. if anything, the case
of Malaysia’s 1MDB example comes to mind, right? China has tried to buy goodwill by buying out of debt corrupt political leaders like Najib in Malaysia.
It’s also done a great deal in Myanmar to prop up the military government there. But it’s not as clear as leveraging debt so much as buying goodwill, which is a familiar approach to great powers around the world.
ERIC OLANDER: I was about to say there’s nothing unique about the Chinese on that one, certainly. The current U.S. administration likes the idea of buying goodwill as well. Just want to talk about the reaction in Southeast Asia, and then we can pull back and see what the
reaction in places like Canberra and the United States has been.
In terms of what you’ve been surveying and looking at, how have Southeast Asian governments responded?
HUNTER MARSTON: They’ve been very understanding, by and large. So Thailand made an
announcement to the effect that this is a sovereign decision of Laos. Vietnam has also been very calm in its response.
Vietnamese Prime Minister Le Minh Huynh went to Vientiane about a week after this announcement, and interestingly, several days after a change of the Laos government, when Salung Say Kamasat became the Vietnamese Prime Minister and his predecessor Son Nac Sai became the Speaker of the National Assembly, I believe. And this cemented, reaffirmed, reinforced Vietnam-Lao ties there. But by and large, Vietnam’s been cautious in
allowing for this development and trying to underscore the importance of Hanoi’s relations with Vientiane rather than chastising them.
ERIC OLANDER: Any word from Singapore, given the fact that Singapore sits right in the nexus on the U.S. and China’s security relationship? They oftentimes host PLA warships and at the same time have service agreements with the U.S. Navy. Any remarks coming out of the Singaporean government as far as you’ve seen?
HUNTER MARSTON: Nothing that I’ve seen, no. I imagine that their defense intelligence
ERIC OLANDER: This has been an area, again, of keen interest in Washington to look at
Chinese basing around the world. One of the things I’ve been pushing back on quite a bit are the narratives that the Chinese want to put
bases in places like West Africa, which, again, we don’t see any evidence. But as you’ve pointed out, the Indian Ocean remains a key area of interest for the Chinese and obviously mainland Southeast Asia and then the South China Sea.
Those are the areas which looks like would be most popular for the Chinese and where they do seem to be getting some traction. What’s been the reaction in some of the Western capitals?
HUNTER MARSTON: I can’t say that the alarm has been as acute this time around as the naval base, which caused quite an uproar, particularly in Washington. When that story broke in 2019, there was a flurry, five-alarm fire, basically, going through Washington. And the security services, U.S. intelligence community really was caught off guard and very paranoid about that development to an extent that I think it took several years of repeated tours of the facility to somewhat assuage that fear that this was going to be an exclusive Chinese base. I think that that never fully went away. There’s still a perception that Ream is something of a Chinese base, even though, we know that Chinese warships have not been the only ones to dock there. The U.S. and Japanese have also, their navies have docked there and various defense officials have received tours of the facilities. Although I’m told that there is still a certain section of Ream Naval Base, which is off limits to foreign militaries. So perhaps China has different access there. And, just as in Singapore, the United States has certain privileges of access to Changi Naval Base that other navies and foreign counterparts do not enjoy.
But in this case of the Banquan Air Facility, it seems like it’s been a pretty quiet international response. And that could just be because Laos is already regarded as something of a Chinese proxy state. It could be that it’s a landlocked state and doesn’t have the same maritime
implications or implications for maritime security that the islands in the South China Sea, Ream Naval Base and other facilities around the Indian Ocean or South Asia would have.
ERIC OLANDER: I’m quite surprised by the muted reaction coming out of not only official Washington, but also the think tanks and many of the chorus that’s getting very excited about, the prospect of bases that were in Africa or in the UAE or whatnot. And then when there actually is a real facility, we don’t hear much. It also might just be a sign of the times that there’s so much coming out of Washington today.
There’s right at the time of the election and just everybody’s distracted and just overwhelmed with everything going on. So this just doesn’t feel like it’s resonating that much. Who knows?
But it is interesting to note that. And what about in Canberra? You spend a lot of time with the Australian folks.
They’re very concerned about China’s security footprint in the Asia-Pacific and the Western Pacific. Any thoughts coming out of like some of the more hawkish think tanks like Aspie and some of the more hawkish views coming out of Australia on this?
HUNTER MARSTON: I haven’t seen a lot of commentary from Aspie. They have one American analyst there who comes from Washington, actually. And I’ve seen her
quoted a bit in media reports, but I haven’t really seen extensive coverage from Aspie on this issue.
Just as we’re not jumping to conclusions here at Lowy. I haven’t actually touched base with my contacts in Australian government on this question, just because I’m in Sydney here and down in Canberra next month. So it’s certainly a question topic I’ll be raising with them when we talk next.
ERIC OLANDER: Okay. Well, one of the things you wrote on X was that clearly the base
could extend the range of PLA fighter jets. But you mentioned that the
bigger story is Beijing’s deepening political influence in mainland
HUNTER MARSTON: That’s right. I don’t think this does a great deal to expand China’s
operational range across Southeast Asia. What it does indicate, though, is China’s political influence in Laos and particularly the deepening of the People’s Revolutionary Party of Laos ties with Beijing.
And what by that is that traditionally, Vietnam has been a very close and trusted friend and security partner to Laos. That dates back to the Revolutionary War and the war for independence against colonial occupying powers in Laos and Vietnam, a shared struggle there that united the two. The Lao government and that of Vietnam were also tied to
So after the 1979 Chinese invasion and occupation of northern Vietnam, it took a long time to rebuild that political trust and ties with China, more than a decade, actually. So China’s influence in Laos is actually more of a recent development since the 1990s. And as China’s economy has grown, its investment across the region has soared; its exports have
And China’s economic presence and influence have allowed it to cultivate stronger political ties and to build trust in the region. And that’s really been very clear in Laos. As I mentioned, China has provided about two-thirds of foreign direct investment in the last decade or so.
It owns the largest share of the country’s debt, and that gives it an enormous amount of political sway. The Lao Revolutionary Party also has strong political ties and a two-plus-two with Beijing that’s recently been elevated or proposed to be elevated to a three-plus-three, which is really indicative of the deepening political and security trust there.
ERIC OLANDER: So just so people are not familiar, two plus two is the foreign minister and the defense minister, and then the three plus three would include who else?
HUNTER MARSTON: Well, it depends country to country. So in the case of Vietnam, this is
something of their, that they traditionally have had for collective leadership, including the chairman of the National Assembly, the prime minister, foreign minister and defense minister. And because the general secretary is currently president and general secretary, I think the three plus three in the case of Vietnam includes the general secretary, foreign minister and defense minister.
In the case of Lao, I think it would follow the same pattern.
ERIC OLANDER: So there in both Vietnam and Lao, there would be a party element to this
in addition to the political element or the state element. Okay.
HUNTER MARSTON: And that’s why a country like Australia can’t replicate this easily. So
we have, Australia has two-plus-twos, but it doesn’t have three-plus-threes with Vietnam or the like.
ERIC OLANDER: While a lot of people focus on the U.S.-China competition, particularly
here in Southeast Asia, up in Beijing, there’s a growing concern now about Japan and the security space. And Japan has been much more active now in Southeast Asia. So you mentioned that the first visit, in fact, to the Ream Naval Base was a Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force ship.
Japan has done a status of forces agreement with the Philippines. The defense minister was recently in Indonesia to sign a new security pact. Takeichi was down in Australia.
And there’s growing concern in Beijing that Japan wants to build a, what many people are speculating is a post-American security architecture that would not necessarily be like it was in the old days, but Japan would play a major force in this. Talking about the security dynamics now in Southeast Asia, what role do you think China is responding to
Japan? And what is the China-Japan dynamic as it relates to Southeast
HUNTER MARSTON: It’s a great question. China’s very wary of Japan’s expanding security
provisions across the region. I think, a lot of that dates back to the
There’s a great groundswell of nationalist vitriol directed against Japan. That’s easy to tap into in China. And I think it’s done for political reasons.
When it comes to actual security provisions, Japan is really one of the most trusted alternate major powers across Southeast Asia. And it’s built that trust and goodwill through decades of official development assistance, the largest provider of ODA to the region since the 1950s, I believe. And today, its development assistance is lagging as countries have actually stopped.
It’s not just Japan. The United States and China have also stopped providing development assistance. And other countries around the world, we’ve seen this trend.
The trend is that development assistance is falling significantly. But Japan also uses the Asian Development Bank as a multilateral mechanism to provide assistance across Southeast Asia. Now, more recently, it stepped up its security assistance with recent legislation regarding what’s called the OSA, the Overseas Security Assistance Act, I believe.
And that has seen Tokyo providing maritime capacity building and technical assistance to countries like the Philippines to expand their Coast Guard capabilities, as well as Vietnam. You mentioned the Reciprocal Access Agreement or Status of Visiting Forces Agreement with the Philippines. And multilateral military exercises have also increased between Japan, the Philippines and Australia.
And those linkages as well as the Quad, which includes Japan, India, Australia and the United States have cemented Japan’s role as a third party major power in this security arena in the latticework, as the Biden administration used to refer to it, of a networked defense community in Asia. So it’s not the same as a NATO model in Europe, but there’s this more loose-knit mini-lateral and multilateral security cooperation, with Japan really playing a lead role there.
ERIC OLANDER: Yeah. As you look forward now, when we think about everything we’ve talked about, the U.S. dynamic, the Japanese dynamic, what the Chinese are trying to achieve in Southeast Asia, what are analysts like yourself looking for next from what China’s doing? Are you anticipating an expansion of the base, or should we expect maybe other of these training arrangements that the Chinese have in Southeast Asia?
HUNTER MARSTON: I think that would be the biggest thing. Does China expand the runway to 3,000 meters, which would allow it to land long-range bombers? And if so, where is it going to send those bombers? it’s not going to threaten Thailand, it’s not going to threaten
Cambodia, in a way. These countries have pretty positive relations. But I think it does allow China to gradually contest the U.S. security presence in the region. If it has that operational range, it expands the ability to fight defensively or offensively even against U.S. assets throughout the region, especially in the South China Sea and the first island chain. But more generally, as you alluded to, I think China could be selling more weapons to countries like Laos and Thailand, where it’s actually replaced the United States as the largest provider of military equipment. Laos is traditionally dependent on Russia a great deal more, like Vietnam has for its arms procurements.
But China’s share of those arms exports to Laos are certainly increasing, and the Air Force is a natural entry point for greater Chinese exports of air equipment.
ERIC OLANDER: I hadn’t thought of this as an extension of a service offer as part of a
sales initiative that the Chinese are doing for weapons around the World. So you sell weapons and then build a training facility to teach them how to use it.
Interesting idea. That’s something I hadn’t really thought about. So but in terms of, again, this is the speculation that goes on in Washington. Are you expecting more of these facilities in Southeast Asia? Or is it just when the opportunity presents itself, they they may jump on it?
HUNTER MARSTON: I think for now, it’s more opportunistic. if this thing were to
materialize in Thailand, it would be a game changer for the United States, in particular, given that it’s an ally and treaty partner, but it no longer truly acts as one. And the two sides really have very little common political ground.
It’s, if anything, the institutions of the two sides’ militaries, which preserves that alliance and operationally, the two still co-host Cobra Gold, the largest multilateral military exercise in Southeast Asia. So that really remains at the bedrock of the alliance. But other than that,
there’s nothing really beyond operations in terms of a guiding worldview or political and security interests that unite Thailand and the United States.
And so therefore, if China were to make inroads, building on its already very strong economic and political ties to replace or supplant the United States security role with Thailand, that would be, I think, a significant change of the balance of power in the region.
ERIC OLANDER: Okay, well, the article is What to Make of China’s New Air Facility in
Laos. It’s really a fantastic piece of work that just gets us to think about what this is and what it isn’t. And again, it’s been a very interesting development that’s happened as we’ve been watching Chinese basing expansions around the world.
It’s very incremental, though. And I think that’s the key point that Hunter’s making. Hunter Marston is the director of the Southeast Asia program at the Lowy Institute and project lead for the Asia Power Index.
Hunter, thank you so much for taking time today to talk to me.
HUNTER MARSTON: Thank you again, Eric. It’s a pleasure to be here.
ERIC OLANDER: Great to have you. And again, we’ll be back again next week with another edition of the China Global South podcast. Of course, if you want to support the work that we’re doing, go to ChinaGlobalSouth.com slash subscribe. Again, this is the only source of its kind available with teams in Asia, Africa and the Middle East following everything that
China is doing from a nonpartisan perspective. Once again, Chinaglobalsouth.com slash subscribe. So for the entire CGSP team around the world, thank you so much for taking the time to listen and to watch.a
